content.text: Every time you plug in an appliance or flip a light switch, you're using a carefully designed electrical system. Understanding domestic electricity—how it's supplied, how plugs and circuits work, and essential safety features—helps us use electricity safely and appreciate the engineering that makes modern life possible.
UK mains electricity is an alternating current (AC) supply at approximately 230 V and 50 Hz. The three wires in a plug are live (brown), neutral (blue), and earth (green/yellow).
Alternating current (AC) means the current direction changes 50 times per second. This is different from batteries, which provide direct current (DC).

The earth wire connects the metal case to the ground (0 V). If a fault causes the live wire to touch the metal case, a large current flows through the low-resistance earth wire to ground. This large current blows the fuse (or trips the MCB), disconnecting the supply and making the appliance safe to touch.
is appropriate (next standard rating above 5.2 A; a 5 A fuse would be too close to the operating current). (calculation & application)

Water is a conductor. In a bathroom, wet hands and skin have much lower resistance, greatly increasing the risk of a fatal electric shock from a 230 V socket. Shaver sockets are allowed because they contain an isolating transformer that limits the current to a safe level, and have no earth connection.

The RCD continuously compares the current flowing in the live wire with the current returning through the neutral wire. Normally these are equal. If current is leaking (e.g. through a person to earth), the live and neutral currents differ. The RCD detects this imbalance (as small as 30 mA) and switches off the supply within about 30 ms -- fast enough to prevent a fatal shock.

If the switch were in the neutral wire, the appliance would still be connected to the live (high-voltage) wire even when switched off. Anyone touching internal parts (e.g. when changing a bulb) could receive a shock from the live wire. Placing the switch in the live wire ensures the dangerous high-voltage connection is broken when the switch is off.

The double-square symbol means the appliance is Class II (double insulated). It has two layers of insulation (or reinforced insulation) between live parts and the user. Because no metal parts can become live, there is no need for an earth wire -- the insulation itself provides the safety protection.
